rows.title: ADR-0036: Results — Decision
rows.summary: `Result<E, T>` with `Ok(value)` / `Err(error)`, never declared.
rows.body: `Result<E, T>` with `Ok(value)` / `Err(error)`, never declared. Inside a function that returns `Result`, errors propagate on their own (no `match`, `try` or `?`); outside, an unhandled `Result` is an error. `.ok(cb)` / `.error(cb)`: a callback returning `Ok`/`Err` transforms or recovers, otherwise it only observes. A `Result` is kept with a variable typed `Result`. An error of another type is a compile error (convert it with `.error(e => Err(...))`). `match` with `Ok(x) ->` / `Err(e) ->`. Each dialect generates its own runtime, without dependencies.

rows.title: ADR-0085: Dragonfly proposals accepted — Decision
rows.summary: 7. Async guards.
body: 7. **Async guards.** `Guard.canActivate()` returns `FutureOr<bool>`; with `~` in its body it is `Future<bool>`.
The router waits for it (its `redirect` stays sync when no guard is async), `AclBuilder` shows `fallback`

`none`; without it, the platform's. It is an enum, not the text `"fade"` the proposal wrote: the editor
completes it and Dart checks it, and `Transition` would clash with bloc's class.
9. **Nested routes with their own back:** a route is nested in the route with the longest address that starts
its own (never `/`). Going to it stacks the parent below, also from a link, so back returns to the parent.
Inside a `shell` tab it stays in that tab. No new argument: the address already says it.
10. **Events from another engine** (workmanager): the `event` kind writes `fromJson`/`toJson`
(json_serializable) and `eventName`. From a background isolate, an event with a name travels as its name
and its JSON text, and `Events.decoder` (registered in `registerModels`) reads it back. So event fields are
JSON types.

rows.summary: 1. No own standard library.
body: 1. **No own standard library.** Math, text, regex, collections, dates, JSON, bytes and async are the target's
(golden rule: no wrapper between the code and the platform; agents already know those APIs). Every area has a
program per target in `examples/stdlib/` printing the same output, run by `tools/stdlib-check.sh`.
2. **Operators** (base grammar, the same for every dialect; each dialect writes them in `[operators]`):
`a ** b` (right associative, above unary minus: `-2 ** 2` is -4), `a ~/ b` (integer division, Dart's token),
`&`, `|`, `^`, `<<`, `>>`, `>>>`, and `^x` for the complement (`~` is await, as in Go). Precedence as in Python
and Dart: comparisons < `|` < `^` < `&` < shifts < `+`. Compound `%= &= |= ^= <<= >>= >>>=`.
3. `>>` and `>>>` are `>` tokens written together, joined by the parser, so `List<List<int>>` keeps working.
4. **Literals:** `0b1010`, `1.5e-3`; **raw text** `r"\d+"` (no escapes nor interpolation), for regular expressions.
5. **Semantics that stay the target's**, documented: `%` (TypeScript keeps the dividend's sign, Dart is never
negative), the integer width of bitwise operators (32 bits in TypeScript, 64 in Dart), rounding of halves.
6. Emitter: `[operators]` templates get the operands' numeric kind (`int`/`double`, for Dart's `pow` returning

(function types), `items_list` (enums), filter `strip_suffix`. A named argument of a decorator is written with
the dialect's `named_arg`. `code_words` reads f-string interpolations and `#` comments.
- **Result:** the file's runtime (`templates/result.tpl`), with explicit covariant TypeVars (a frozen dataclass is
invariant from Python 3.13 on because of `__replace__`).

and others, and Dragonfly's own backend in Rust.
- `mobile`: `flutter` (Dart); later `react-native`, `kotlin-multiplatform`, native Android...
- `web`: none yet; `react`, `vue`, `angular` planned.

as targets for a single `.nuc` without Dragonfly).

body: - **Isar**: v3 is unmaintained against current Flutter, v4 unfinished. **Drift / sqflite / sqlite3**: real SQL and
SQLCipher, but web needs a wasm bundle and a worker copied into every app, and drift adds its own code generation
per table on top of json_serializable; the backend's query vocabulary is covered without SQL at mobile sizes.
**Hive v2 (original)** is frozen; `hive_ce` is its maintained fork with the same API, pure Dart, web and encryption
built in. **sembast**: queries built in, but no encryption without a third package.
- **A `entity` kind in mobile**: a second kind for the same model doubled every model (an http model and a table
model); the user asked for the minimum annotations on the model the GET returns.
- **`<method>AsLocal()` reading the table by the method's parameters** (`getOne(id)` → `find(id)`): correct only when
a parameter is the key; `search(name)` or `getPage(page)` would need a per-method mapping. Remembering which rows
each call answered works for every signature and still returns fresh rows.
- **A plugin `local`** with the package added only when used: `hive_ce` is pure Dart and small; a plugin would add a
line to `config.nuc` for a feature two annotations already declare.

body: - Easier: offline reading with two words (`saveLocal = true`, `@primary`), the backend's query vocabulary on the
device, a local-only repository without new kinds, generated tests that check each twin answers without a request.
- Harder / limits: a GET that answers a model without `@primary` under `saveLocal` fails at its first call with a
`StateError` that names the fix (the generated tests catch it; no compile-time diagnostic yet); `local = false`
on a method does not opt out of `saveLocal` (templates have no value comparison); `isNull` of the backend is not
a mobile operator (the word is the `flutter_test` matcher already in the dialect's auto-imports, so a `[functions]`
shortcut is refused by N0204); `hive_ce` keeps a box in memory, so a table is for the data a phone shows, not for
millions of rows; `@created`/`@updated` are ISO-8601 texts; a backend entity's `@column` options (`length`,
`unique`, `index`) have no equivalent in a document store; turning `encrypted` on or off after the first run needs
the tables cleared (a box is read with the cipher it was written with); on web the key lives in the browser's
storage, weaker than a phone's keystore.

body: 1. **A model with `@primary` (or `@generated`) has a local table.** The same words as a backend entity: `@primary`

backend (default: the model's name in snake_case; the box is `dragonfly_<name>`). `@column` has no meaning in a
document store (the JSON name, `@key`, is the column) and is not part of the mobile platform. The flutter dialect
writes `static final LocalTable<M> table` in the model and registers it at startup with its component
(`Local.register(M.table, component: 'characters')` in `registerDragonfly`).
2. **`@repository(saveLocal = true)`, or `@get(local = true)` on one method.** A GET that answers a model with a
table (or a list of them; not `Page<Character>`, which has no key) passes `local: 'Repo.method'` to `send`: the
decoded rows go to the model's table and a calls table remembers which rows that call (url + query) answered.
The transpiler writes the twin **`<method>AsLocal()`**, same signature and return type, that reads those rows as
they are now (`recall`) and never sends a request; without a previous answer it is `Err(E(message))` for a
`Result` method and a thrown `NotFound` otherwise.

body: - Easier: a mobile or web app over a Nuclear backend writes no model and no repository; the rules travel; a change
in the API is caught at build time; the editors read every project's endpoints from the same file (ADR-0099).
- Limits: entities travel only when a route returns them; generics in a route's answer (`Page<Task>`) are

`contract::generate`); two contracts that export the same model name clash (each is a top-level declaration);
versions are shown, not enforced (a stale copy is not a warning yet, plan 003 F5).

rows.summary: A backend written in Nuclear defines its models and routes once; every app that calls it wrote the same models and a repository per controller again, by hand, with nothing checking the copies.
body: A backend written in Nuclear defines its models and routes once; every app that calls it wrote the same models and
a repository per controller again, by hand, with nothing checking the copies. A renamed field or a changed path
compiled on both sides and failed at run time; the validation rules stayed in the backend; an agent spent its

the **description** of the API traveling from one to the other, the way OpenAPI, `.proto` files or tRPC do it.

rows.title: ADR-0098: Shared contracts: a backend publishes what it exposes, a client generates its models and repositories — Decision
rows.summary: 1. Every project writes its contract.
body: 1. **Every project writes its contract.** `nuclear build`, `nuclear check`, `dragonfly build` and the editors (the
same call that writes the project card, `project::write_metadata`) write `.nuclear/contract.json`: the models
(fields, Nuclear types, optionality, defaults, JSON names, validation rules, the key field, doc comments) and,
for a backend, the controllers with their routes (verb, path, parameters with where they go, body, answer,
error type, status); for a mobile or web app, the repositories with the calls they make. The contract is in
Nuclear's notation and is **the same whatever the dialect** (checked by a test with `nestjs` and `fastapi`).
2. **A backend also writes OpenAPI 3.1** (`.nuclear/openapi.json`, from the contract: paths, parameters, request
bodies, responses, schemas with the rules, doc comments as summaries). Both files are copied into the output
folder, and the runtimes serve them at `GET /.nuclear/contract.json` and `GET /.nuclear/openapi.json`, so a
client that is not Nuclear (Swagger UI, a generator, an HTTP tool) reads the API as built.
3. **A client declares the backends it talks to** in its manifest: `contracts(tasks_api = "../tasks_api")` (a path:
the backend built next to it, monorepo or a sibling checkout) or `contracts(tasks_api = "https://api.x.com")`

body: - An entity reads like a TypeORM entity in both backend dialects; the key is one word on backend and mobile.
- The rules of the relation decorators are data of the dialect, so a new backend dialect gets them by writing templates.
- The column name of a relation (`project_id`) and the join table name (`<owner table>_<field>`) are conventions, the

circular imports) and its runtime `Entity` keeps relations given to the constructor; in Dart `Page<T>` is the
runtime's `PageOf<T>` (`[types] Page = "PageOf"`: Flutter has its own `Page`; a project's own `Page` keeps its name).

`[decorators.fields]` (`optional`, `list`, `target` = a decorator the field's type must have, `sibling` = a field that
must exist, `inverse` = an argument that names a field of the type); templates get `tinfo.decor` (the decorators of the

rows.title: ADR-0100: Backend data: one key decorator, TypeORM relations, pagination, transactions, migrations — 2. Relations: TypeORM's decorators
rows.summary: The join table defaults to `<owner table>_<field>` (`tasks_tags`), with the columns `<entity>_id` of both sides.
body: The join table defaults to `<owner table>_<field>` (`tasks_tags`), with the columns `<entity>_id` of both sides. The
related type comes from the field's type, so it is not repeated in the decorator (TypeORM writes `() => Project`
because TypeScript erases types; Nuclear has them). The join column is a field of its own (`projectId`), as TypeORM
allows: it is set without loading the other row (`Task(title = t, projectId = id)`) and it is in the JSON answer.
**Rules, checked at compile time (N0308):** a relation field is optional (`?`: it is there only when loaded); its type
is an entity (a list for `@oneToMany`/`@manyToMany`, one for `@manyToOne`/`@oneToOne`); `@manyToOne` (and `@oneToOne`
with `@joinColumn`) needs the field `<name>Id`; `inverse` names a field of the related entity.
**Loading is explicit**, TypeORM's `relations`, one more step of the query builder; an unloaded relation is absent
from the JSON answer (never `null`, never a lazy query):
```nuclear
repository ProjectRepository
withTasks(id: int) Result<NotFound, Project>
where({ "id": id })
relations("tasks")
getOne()
Saving writes what the entity holds: the join column of a `@manyToOne`, and the rows of the join table when a
`@manyToMany` list is set (`task.tags = [a, b]` then `save(task)`), the same in both dialects.

@entity("projects")
entity Project()
@primary(generated = true)
id: int
name: string
@oneToMany(inverse = "project")

@entity("tasks")
entity Task()
@primary(generated = true)
id: int
title: string
@manyToOne(inverse = "tasks", onDelete = "cascade")
project?: Project
projectId: int                 // the join column of `project` (projectId?: int → a task may have no project)

`Page<T>` (`items: T[]`, `page` from 1, `size`, `total`, `pages`) is a class of the runtimes; `paginate` is one more

body: ```nuclear
usecase MoveTasks(tasks: TaskRepository, projects: ProjectRepository)
@transactional
exec(from: int, to: int) Result<Error, int>
~projects.find(to)
moved = ~tasks.where({ "projectId": from }).update({ "projectId": to })

Every repository call inside the method joins one transaction of the default database; an `Err` result or a thrown
error rolls it back, an `Ok` commits it. fastapi: an `AsyncSession` in a `ContextVar`; nestjs: a sequelize
transaction in an `AsyncLocalStorage`; the repositories of both runtimes read it, so nothing else changes.

body: - fastapi: Alembic. `make` brings an empty SQLite in memory to the last migration and lets autogenerate write the
difference, in batch mode (SQLite cannot alter a column; the other databases run the same file);
`dragonfly.migrate` writes the folder's `env.py` once; `alembic_version` lists what is applied.

migrations are listed in `SequelizeMeta` (sequelize-cli's table). umzug was not needed for that.
- A field default (`done: boolean = false`) is also the column's SQL default in both (Python's `column(default=...)`
sets `server_default`), so adding a non-null column to a table with rows works.
- Renames show as a drop and an add; `make` warns of every drop; the file is the project's to edit.

rows.summary: The local agent treated every request the same way.
body: The local agent treated every request the same way. The planner had one prompt for everything, and the Loop ran the

first* as if it were a feature. The spec's `Use case` field was kept and changed nothing. The knowledge base had 22

A small model follows steps better than it chooses them. So choosing what to do with a request cannot be the
model's work.

Tools before models, in every strategy: a generator writes what is standard; the compiler's exact fixes (`nuclear fix`) come before any repair; a rename is done by a tool (`Workspace.renamed`: every file that writes the name as a word, with the new one in its place, and with it the project's…
body: 6. **Tools before models, in every strategy**: a generator writes what is standard; the compiler's exact fixes
(`nuclear fix`) come before any repair; a rename is done by a tool (`Workspace.renamed`: every file that writes
the name as a word, with the new one in its place, and with it the project's names built from it, `NewBook` and
`BookRepository` for `Book`) and no model writes; the files a change starts in are found
by the project's declarations, not planned. A model writes only a piece of one file that no tool can write.
7. **The Loop follows the strategy.** The analysis is the last step of the *Specification* stage. Then: the stages
the strategy has no use for are skipped; *Generate* runs the spec's own resources and the calls the analysis
derived; *Plan* takes the pieces the tools gave, and asks the planner only when the strategy's pieces come from a
plan; *Code* writes a piece a tool already wrote as it is, and afterwards wires each use case the coder wrote with
`dragonfly gen usecase` (its alias and, when the spec's sentence gives it, its route); *Verification*, for a bug,
repairs the file the failure names whoever wrote it, and never the test. A Developer without an analyst leaves the
run as it was: every stage.

rows.title: ADR-0105: A strategy for each kind of request — Decision
rows.summary: 1. A strategy is a row of the knowledge base (`strategy:<name>`, type `strategy`, on the playbooks shelf): one per kind of request a user makes.
body: 1. **A strategy is a row of the knowledge base** (`strategy:<name>`, type `strategy`, on the playbooks shelf): one
per kind of request a user makes. It holds how the kind is recognised, its plan step by step with the tool of
every step, and what it asks of a run. Changing how a kind of request is handled is changing a row, never code.
2. **The kinds of request**, in five families:
| Family | Strategies |
| create | `system`, `project`, `component`, `resource-api`, `resource-db`, `client-of-backend`, `interface`, `repository`, `usecase`, `endpoint`, `declaration` |
| change | `member`, `refactor-rename`, `refactor-move-extract`, `refactor-architecture`, `data-migration`, `configuration`, `remove` |
| fix | `bug-compile`, `bug-failing-test`, `bug-behaviour`, `bug-runtime`, `bug-data-contract`, `bug-interface`, `bug-environment` |
| verify and explain | `tests`, `security-review`, `document`, `question`, `operate` |
| beyond | `beyond` |
3. **What a strategy row says**, besides its card for people and lead models:

rows.title: ADR-0105: A strategy for each kind of request — Decision
rows.summary: Decision
body: | Field | Meaning |
| `data.signals` | regular expressions over the request: its exact signs (a diagnostic code, a test's output, `rename A to B`, a `GET <url>` line) |
| `meta.triggers` | the words that point to it |
| `data.target` | `existing`: the request names a declaration the project has; `new`: one it has not |
| `asks` | how people ask for it, in English and Spanish: found by meaning |
| `data.mode` | `write`, `repair` (the compiler's errors drive), `fix` (a failing test drives), `review`, `answer`, `commands`, `lead` |
| `data.stages` | the stages of the Loop it runs; empty: this kind of request is not a run |

| `data.pieces` | where its pieces come from: `plan` (the planner splits what is left), `declaring` (the files that declare what the request names), `naming` (every file that writes a name: a rename), `none` |
| `data.generators` | the generators it calls |
| `data.needs` | the facts it cannot start without, each with its question for the user |
| `data.lead` | `frontier` when it needs a model that understands several files at once |

rows.title: ADR-0105: A strategy for each kind of request — Decision
rows.summary: 4. The selection asks no model (`POST /v1/strategy`, `nuclear-graph strategy "<request>"`, MCP `graph_strategy`).
body: 4. **The selection asks no model** (`POST /v1/strategy`, `nuclear-graph strategy "<request>"`, MCP
`graph_strategy`). An exact sign of the request outweighs any closeness of meaning; meaning decides between
strategies with no exact sign, or the same ones; whether the project has the names the request writes moves the
score. The answer says which signs chose the strategy. A run of the Loop cannot follow a strategy without stages
(a question, a command): such a strategy comes first for a run only when an exact sign chose it. A spec may name
its strategy itself (`- Strategy: usecase`).
5. **The analyst** (`nuclear-developer`, `POST /developer/analyze`) runs before anything is generated or planned,
in fixed steps: the project's files say which names of the request exist; the graph gives the strategy; the
strategy gives the stages, the source of the pieces and the facts it needs. A model is asked for one thing only:
the resources a request in plain words describes (`component | Name | fields | source | actions`). Each line
becomes a `dragonfly gen resource` call and is kept only if its `--dry-run` accepts it. A fact the request lacks is
a question for the user and stops the run: nothing is guessed.

rows.title: ADR-0105: A strategy for each kind of request — Limits
rows.summary: 11 cases, 4 of the 5 that ask the model.
body: - The analyst's one model call (the resources of a plain-words request) is measured by `eval/run.py analyze`: 10 of
11 cases, 4 of the 5 that ask the model. A model asked about a request that lists no field invents them, so it is
asked only when the request lists some, and its answer is held to that list: the number of fields must be the
request's, it is asked once more when it is not, and left out (the fields are then asked to the user) when the
second answer fails too. The case that fails is that one: a field dropped twice. Types it reads from words (`total`
as `double`) are shown in the *Generate* step, to be checked there.

rows.title: ADR-0105: A strategy for each kind of request — Limits
rows.summary: small embedding model does less well than an exact sign.
body: - The selection reads words: a request that names its kind in an unusual way is classified by meaning alone, which a
small embedding model does less well than an exact sign. Its test set is 62 requests; a wrong reading is fixed by a
sign or a question in the row.
- `refactor-move-extract`, `remove` and `beyond` need a lead: the local agents do their mechanical steps only.
- A rename by the tool covers a declaration's name and the declarations built from it by a word before or after
(the platform binds a repository to its entity by its name, so an entity renamed alone compiles and fails when it
runs). That also takes a declaration that only starts with the name (`OrderLine` with `Order`): the analysis lists
every name it changes. A field or a method is renamed by hand (the same word may be another declaration's member);
the file of a renamed declaration keeps its path; a plural (`ListBooks`) and an alias of the facade stay. A rename
runs no security review: it writes no new logic.
- A bug whose failure names only its test stops at *Verification*: where the cause is needs a lead or the user.
- The Loop writes files and never deletes one.
- Still by hand or by a model, with no generator: relations in a stored resource, the tests of a backend resource
over another API, what a screen shows of a use case added with `gen usecase` (mobile, web).

rows.title: ADR-0106: The AI services come with the installer — Decision
rows.summary: 7. Remote agents only is a choice of the first step: nothing runs on the machine.
body: 7. **Remote agents only** is a choice of the first step: nothing runs on the machine. The MCP server is installed
alone (`nuclear-graph[mcp]`, 33 MB instead of 405), offers the generators, the compiler, the command line and the
internet tools, takes away the tools that need the graph or the local developer, and its instructions ask the
model to write what the generators do not. The wizard says what that costs: every line is paid tokens.
8. **The choice is one file**: `~/.config/nuclearlang/ai.env` (`%APPDATA%\nuclearlang\ai.env`), `KEY=value` lines:
the mode, the profile, its models. The services start with it; the Loop and the editor take their default models
from it; the MCP server reads the mode from it. A model set in the editor's settings wins there and is written to
the file when the editor restarts a service.
9. **The services start at every login**, with the system's own means and no administrator rights: two systemd user
units on Linux (`nuclear-graph`, `nuclear-developer`, restarted when they fail), two launch agents on macOS, a
script in the Startup folder on Windows. The editor's Start and Restart go through them. A system without a user
service manager gets the services started now and is told so. A service started by hand that holds the port stops
the set-up with the command that stops it.

rows.title: ADR-0106: The AI services come with the installer — Decision
rows.summary: Every local profile also downloads `embeddinggemma` (0.6 GB, counted above), which makes the graph's vectors.
body: Every local profile also downloads `embeddinggemma` (0.6 GB, counted above), which makes the graph's vectors. No model is larger than 3B parameters of effective size.
`lite` and the assistant's part of `medium` are not fully measured yet: the wizard says so in their cards.
5. **What the services need is data too**: NuclearLang itself, `uv` (the Python environments; it brings its own
Python) and Ollama (the local profiles only). Each is found by its command, or installed by its own installer in a
terminal the user sees (Ollama's asks for a password on Linux), or by hand from its page: the wizard checks every
three seconds and sees it once it is there.

rows.title: ADR-0106: The AI services come with the installer — Decision
rows.summary: 1. Every release archive carries the code of the services (`ai/nuclear-graph`, `ai/nuclear-developer` with its knowledge base: 5 MB).
body: 1. **Every release archive carries the code of the services** (`ai/nuclear-graph`, `ai/nuclear-developer` with its
knowledge base: 5 MB). What is large is downloaded by the set-up, after the user chose: the Python packages
(≈ 550 MB) and the models. Nothing of a model fits a release (a release file is at most 2 GB).
2. **One set-up, two fronts.** `aiSetup.ts` reads the machine, finds what is installed and runs the steps. The editor
shows it as a wizard (*Nuclear: Set Up the AI Services*; offered once on a machine never set up; a button in
*Settings and integrations*); a terminal as `nuclear-loop setup`, which the installers call at their end. Nothing
is downloaded before the user presses Install or answers the question.
3. **The wizard's steps**: this machine (processor, memory, GPU, free disk) and where the agents run; the profile;
what it needs; the installation, with the progress of each step and *Try again* from the step that failed.

rows.title: ADR-0106: The AI services come with the installer — Decision
rows.summary: 6. Ollama stays the program that runs the models.
body: 6. **Ollama stays the program that runs the models.** Looked at on 2026-11-13: llama.cpp's own server, LM Studio,
MLX, vLLM. Ollama, LM Studio, Jan and others run the same engine (llama.cpp), so on the same model and quantization
the published differences are a few percent, and the comparisons found disagree with each other; MLX is clearly
faster on Apple silicon, and Ollama has had an MLX engine there since March 2026. What decides is the rest: one
installer per system that leaves a service running, models pulled by name, a model loaded when asked and freed
afterwards, chat and embeddings behind one address, an open licence, no window that must stay open. llama.cpp's
server would be ours to package for every system and GPU, with the models' files and memory managed by us; LM
Studio is not open and is an application; vLLM is for GPU servers. Where the models run is one address
(`OLLAMA_URL`): changing the program later touches the Developer's connection, not the set-up.

rows.title: ADR-0106: The AI services come with the installer — Limits
rows.summary: Ollama.
body: - The set-up is in VS Code and in a terminal. Android Studio has no wizard: `nuclear-loop setup`.
- macOS and Windows are written and not run: the launch agents, the Startup script, `winget` and Homebrew for
Ollama. Only Linux with systemd ran.
- No GPU is recognised except NVIDIA's (`nvidia-smi`) and Apple silicon: on other machines the set-up says that no
GPU with memory of its own was found, although Ollama may use an integrated one.
- The first load of the knowledge base asks Ollama for an embedding of every row: about two minutes.
- The models are Ollama's files in the user's folder: several users of one machine download them once each.

rows.title: Plan: agents master Nuclear and Dragonfly without spending tokens — 1. Goal
rows.summary: An agent (Claude Code or another) writes correct Nuclear/Dragonfly on the first or second try, without having been trained on the language, and the cost of "teaching" it is much lower than the token savings of the `.nuc` itself.
body: An agent (Claude Code or another) writes correct Nuclear/Dragonfly on the first or second try, without having
been trained on the language, and the cost of "teaching" it is much lower than the token savings of the `.nuc`
itself.
No model is trained nor fine-tuned: it is not possible with Claude and it is not needed. The knowledge arrives
three ways: **minimal context** (what changes compared with Dart/TS), **on-demand lookups** (the CLI already
answers everything) and **compiler feedback** (errors that say how to fix themselves).

rows.title: Plan: agents master Nuclear and Dragonfly without spending tokens — Success metric

body: Measured with the evaluation suite (F1), against today's baseline:
| Metric | Target |

| Total tokens per task | ≤ the baseline's, even loading the skill |

rows.title: Plan: agents master Nuclear and Dragonfly without spending tokens — 2. Diagnosis (measured on 2026-10-27 on `flutter/rick_and_morty`)
rows.summary: About 4 times less than the equivalent Dart.
body: **The language already saves what it promises:**
| | Size | Approx. tokens |
| The project's `.nuc` source (37 files) | 18.7 KB | ~5k |
| Generated Dart (48 files) | 75.4 KB | ~20k |
About **4 times less** than the equivalent Dart.
**The problem is what explaining it costs:**
| Document | Size | Approx. tokens |
| `nuclear spec` (base) | 71 KB | ~18k |
| `nuclear spec --dialect flutter` | 196 KB | ~50k |
| `nuclear help flutter` | 103 KB | ~26k |
| the whole `spec/` | 280 KB | ~70k |
Loading the Flutter spec costs **2.5 times the whole project**. Principle 5 of `nuclear-base.md` ("the whole spec
fits in the context") holds today only in theory: it fits, but it takes all the savings. The spec is the right
reference for humans and for the transpiler; the agent needs something else.
**What already exists and works as it is** (no need to reinvent it):

rows.title: Plan: agents master Nuclear and Dragonfly without spending tokens — 2. Diagnosis (measured on 2026-10-27 on `flutter/rick_and_morty`)
rows.summary: notation.
body: - `nuclear check <file|folder> --json` and `dragonfly check --json`: errors + architecture rules.
- `nuclear defs show|search <Name> --dialect flutter`: the API of Flutter, Dragonfly and the packages in Nuclear
notation. `defs show Text` takes about 700 tokens: a cheap, precise lookup.
- `nuclear help <topic>`: a guide split into chapters of 1–4k tokens.
- `tools/spec-check/check.py`: checks that the Nuclear → target examples are the real output.
- `dragonfly make`: generates the skeleton of each piece (screen, usecase, repository...), so the agent does not
write the structure from scratch.
- LSP + VS Code extension (subproject `editors/`).
**Gaps found** (tested with `nuclear check --dialect flutter`):

rows.title: Plan: agents master Nuclear and Dragonfly without spending tokens — 2. Diagnosis (measured on 2026-10-27 on `flutter/rick_and_morty`)
rows.summary: The last two are the most serious: the error shows up only in `flutter analyze`, on the generated Dart and with lines the agent never wrote.
body: | What an agent coming from Dart writes | Result today | Problem |
| `Text("a", style: TextStyle())` | N0013 + `fix: replace ':' with ' ='` | ✅ good |
| `return Text("a");` | N0009 + `fix: delete ';'` | ✅ good |
| `build(...) Widget {` | N0013 `expected end of line, found '{'` | no hint: "blocks go by indentation" |
| `Widget build(BuildContext context)` | N0013 `expected end of line, found '('` | no hint: "the return type goes at the end" |
| `x = await g()` | N0013 `found 'g'` | no hint: "use `~g()`" |
| `var x = 3` | N0013 `found 'x'` | no hint: "write `x = 3`" |
| `class Bar extends Foo` | N0201 + a list of 35 kinds | no hint: "`Bar: Foo`" or the right kind |
| `Textt("a")` | **no error** | nonexistent constructor: an invisible hallucination |
| `Text("a", styl = TextStyle())` | **no error** | nonexistent argument: an invisible hallucination |
The last two are the most serious: the error shows up only in `flutter analyze`, on the generated Dart and with
lines the agent never wrote.
There is no agent integration either: `dragonfly new` generates no `CLAUDE.md`, `AGENTS.md`, skill nor hooks.

rows.title: Plan: agents master Nuclear and Dragonfly without spending tokens — 3. Features
rows.summary: Ordered by the work sequence.
rows.body: Ordered by the work sequence. Each one with its "done" criterion.

rows.title: Plan: agents master Nuclear and Dragonfly without spending tokens — F1. Evaluation suite and baseline (first: without it, there is no way…
rows.summary: location", "a usecase with a 5-minute cache", "a form with validation", "a global event when the network changes".
body: - 10–15 real tasks on a copy of `rick_and_morty`. Examples: "add search to episodes", "a detail screen for a
location", "a usecase with a 5-minute cache", "a form with validation", "a global event when the network
changes". Also 2–3 NestJS tasks so it is not biased towards Flutter.
- A script that runs each task with `claude -p --output-format json` (clean, headless session) and records:
input/output tokens, turns, number of red `check`s and whether it ended green.
- Location: `tools/agent-eval/` (tasks in TOML, runner in Python like `spec-check`).
- **Done when:** the baseline without the skill is stored in `tools/agent-eval/results/baseline.json`.

rows.title: Plan: agents master Nuclear and Dragonfly without spending tokens — F2. A differences sheet: `nuclear spec --brief [--dialect <d>]`
rows.summary: The center of the plan.
body: The center of the plan. A short document (target: ≤ 4k tokens with Flutter) written **for someone who already
knows Dart/TypeScript**. It includes only what changes:
- A table of rules: blocks by indentation, return type at the end, `name = value` in arguments, `~` for await
and automatic async, implicit return, `if`/`match` as values, `Result`/`Ok`/`Err` with propagation, aliases
`f() = Module.method`, constructors `(dep: Type)`, kinds instead of `class`.
- 10–15 **Nuclear → Dart pairs** chosen from what is used most, generated from the transpiler's real output
(checked with `spec-check`, as today).
- Dragonfly kinds in one line each (`repository`, `usecase`, `statemanager`, `stateless`, `appcomponent`...) and
the architecture rules (screen → component → usecase → repository).
- "How to look up the rest": `nuclear help <topic>`, `nuclear defs show X`, `dragonfly make`.
Source: `spec/<dialect>.brief.md` next to each spec, embedded with `include_str!` like the other topics.
`--brief` concatenates the briefs of the dialect's chain (flutter → dart → base), like `spec`.
- **Done when:** `nuclear spec --brief --dialect flutter` measures ≤ 4k tokens, `spec-check` gives 0 problems on
the briefs, and an agent with only the brief solves a simple F1 task.

rows.title: Plan: agents master Nuclear and Dragonfly without spending tokens — F3. Claude Code skill + `AGENTS.md`
rows.summary: `nuclear.toml`) and the work cycle: 1. `dragonfly make ...` for the skeleton.
body: - A `nuclear` skill (folder `SKILL.md` + references). Its body is short: when it applies (`*.nuc`,
`nuclear.toml`) and the work cycle:
1. `dragonfly make ...` for the skeleton.
2. Write following the brief.
3. `dragonfly check --json` → fix until green.
4. On a doubtful API: `nuclear defs show/search`, never guess.
- The brief **is not copied** into the skill: the skill asks for `nuclear spec --brief --dialect <d>`, so it is
never out of date with the installed binary.
- `install.sh` installs the skill in `~/.claude/skills/nuclear/` (option `--no-agent` to skip it).
- `dragonfly new` generates in the project an `AGENTS.md` of 10–20 lines (it works for any agent, not only
Claude) and a `CLAUDE.md` that imports it with `@AGENTS.md`. A `dragonfly agent init` command is added for
existing projects like `rick_and_morty`.
- **Done when:** in a new project, Claude Code activates the skill by itself when it touches a `.nuc`, and the F1
tasks have fewer errors than the baseline.

rows.title: Plan: agents master Nuclear and Dragonfly without spending tokens — F4. Automatic check hook
rows.summary: A Claude Code `PostToolUse` hook for `Edit|Write` on `*.nuc`: it runs `nuclear check <file> --json` (or the project's) and, if there are errors, gives them back to the agent in the same turn.
body: A Claude Code `PostToolUse` hook for `Edit|Write` on `*.nuc`: it runs `nuclear check <file> --json` (or the
project's) and, if there are errors, gives them back to the agent in the same turn. The agent does not have to
remember to check.
- Installed with the skill (F3) inside the project's `.claude/settings.json` through `dragonfly agent init`.
- Compact output: only code, line, message and `fix`, without the source code block. Few tokens.
- **Done when:** a `.nuc` with an error, edited by the agent, gets the diagnostic without the agent asking.

rows.title: Plan: agents master Nuclear and Dragonfly without spending tokens — F5. Diagnostics with fixes for Dart/TS habits
rows.summary: In the parser/diagnostics (`nuclear-syntax`, `nuclear-diag`), detect and give a `fix`: `spec/diagnostics.md` (the test `every_code_is_documented` requires it).
body: In the parser/diagnostics (`nuclear-syntax`, `nuclear-diag`), detect and give a `fix`:
| Pattern | Suggested message |
| `{` at the end of a header | `blocks use indentation, not braces` + fix: delete `{` / `}` |
| `Type name(params)` | `the return type goes after the parameters: name(params) Type` |
| `await expr` | `use ~expr (async is automatic)` |
| `var/final/let/const x = ` in a body | `assign directly: x = ...` |
| `class X extends Y` | `use a kind or 'X: Y'` + the most likely kinds, not all 35 |
| `new X(...)` | `NuclearLang does not use 'new'` |
- Probably N0013/N0201 are reused adding `fix`/`help`, or new codes are created and documented in
`spec/diagnostics.md` (the test `every_code_is_documented` requires it).
- **Done when:** each pattern has a test, `cargo test` and `cargo clippy` are green, and the F1 tasks show fewer
correction turns.

rows.title: Plan: agents master Nuclear and Dragonfly without spending tokens — F6. Validation against type definitions (the strongest defense against…
rows.summary: The transpiler already loads the defs (`Dialect.defs`, `index.json`) for auto-imports and overrides.
body: The transpiler already loads the defs (`Dialect.defs`, `index.json`) for auto-imports and overrides. They are
also used to validate:
- `PascalCase(...)` that is not in the file, the project nor the defs → an error with "did you mean `Text`?"
(edit distance over the known names).
- A named argument the constructor or method does not have → an error with the valid parameters.
- (Optional, later) A nonexistent member on a known type: `Icons.casinoo`.
Available base (added by another session, ADR-0065–0069): project defs are added with
`Loader::add_defs(&mut Dialect, &project::defs_lock(root))` (reads `build/defs.lock`, refs `name@version`),
`nuclear_dialect::defs_cache_dir()` and `Package::from_project`. The validation must look up the dialect
**after** `add_defs`; otherwise the project's third-party packages (`dragonfly flutter add`) would give false
positives. The LSP already calls `add_defs` before `project::build`.

rows.title: Plan: agents master Nuclear and Dragonfly without spending tokens — F6. Validation against type definitions (the strongest defense against…
rows.summary: Care: nothing is reported: zero false positives before full coverage.
body: Care:
- Only when the type resolves with certainty. If the module stays `open` (unknown base or a whole-module `use`),
nothing is reported: zero false positives before full coverage.
- It goes in N01xx (resolver), documented in `spec/diagnostics.md`.
- If `ast.rs` changes, tell `editors/` which variants changed (AGENTS.md rule 7).
- **Done when:** `Textt("a")` and `styl = ...` fail in `nuclear check`; the 37 files of `rick_and_morty`, the
examples and the golden files still have no errors; `cargo test` is green.

rows.summary: Repeat F1 with everything on.
body: Repeat F1 with everything on. Tune the brief according to where agents still fail: each repeated error is a
missing line in the brief or a missing `fix` in a diagnostic.

rows.title: Plan: agents master Nuclear and Dragonfly without spending tokens — 4. Out of scope (for now)
rows.summary: schemas.
body: - **Fine-tuning or training:** not possible with Claude; context + compiler give the same practical result.
- **MCP server:** the CLI already answers everything through Bash, and an MCP adds fixed tokens with its tool
schemas. It is reconsidered only if an agent without a shell needs it.
- **`llms.txt`, a public site and example repositories:** the way for future models to learn Nuclear by
themselves. Worth it when the language is published, but it takes months and does not help today.
- **Rewriting the specs:** they stay the source of truth; the brief is a short view on top.

rows.summary: Phases 2–4 have the highest impact for the least code (a few days).
body: | Phase | Feature | Where | Notes |
| 1 | F1 baseline | `nuclearlang/tools/agent-eval/` | before touching anything |
| 2 | F2 brief | `spec/*.brief.md`, `crates/nuclear-cli` | `spec-check` on the briefs |
| 3 | F3 skill + AGENTS.md | `install.sh`, `cli/` (subproject, its own context) | `dragonfly agent init` |

| 5 | F5 diagnostics | `crates/nuclear-syntax`, `nuclear-diag`, `spec/diagnostics.md` | tests per pattern |

| 7 | F7 measurement | `tools/agent-eval/` | compare with the baseline |

Repository rules that apply (see `AGENTS.md`): everything in English, each new diagnostic documented,

rows.summary: A developer tells a coding agent (Claude, Codex, OpenCode) "turn Crystal and Amber into Dragonfly", the agent creates the dialect following Nuclear's rules as we did with `flutter` and `nestjs`, pushes it to a repository, and anyone uses it with `dragonfly crystal/amber new`.
body: A developer tells a coding agent (Claude, Codex, OpenCode) "turn Crystal and Amber into Dragonfly", the agent
creates the dialect following Nuclear's rules as we did with `flutter` and `nestjs`, pushes it to a repository,
and anyone uses it with `dragonfly crystal/amber new`.
- The user **does not program nor edit the dialect by hand**: they describe the *what for* and review.
Everything goes through the agent.
- The agent **cannot leave** the rules, philosophy nor restrictions of Nuclear and Dragonfly
(`spec/dialects.md` §8.4). What cannot be expressed is reported; it is not faked.
**Out of scope (postponed):** kinds, decorators and shortcuts of each project (detecting repeated code,
extension points in the framework's templates, derived kinds). They are taken up later; the project dialect
format of `spec/dialects.md` §7 stays the same and is not extended.

rows.summary: `nuclear spec [--dialect]` (the full contract for agents); `nuclear build --dialect <path>`.
body: - Declarative dialects (TOML + templates) with inheritance; `nuclear dialect check --json`;
`nuclear spec [--dialect]` (the full contract for agents); `nuclear build --dialect <path>`.
- `spec/dialects.md` §8: purpose, what a dialect can do, process, **restrictions** and the done criterion. It is
the source of truth the agent reads.
- User tutorial: `docs/dialects/create-with-agent.md`.
- `tools/spec-check/check.py` checks that a spec's equivalences are the real output, but only inside the

rows.title: Plan: new dialects created by agents — Gaps
rows.summary: 1. The `dragonfly` CLI has Flutter written in Rust (`Manifest::infer(root, "flutter", ...)`, `doctor`, the SDK, the pubspec, build/run/test).
body: 1. **The `dragonfly` CLI has Flutter written in Rust** (`Manifest::infer(root, "flutter", ...)`, `doctor`, the
SDK, the pubspec, build/run/test). A new dialect cannot have its own `dragonfly <d> new`.
2. **Dragonfly's rules as a concept are mixed with Flutter** in `spec/flutter.md` (§1, §3, §4, §6). An agent
building `crystal/amber` has no neutral spec of what Dragonfly is.
3. **There is no example checking outside the repository**: a user's agent has no `spec-check`.
4. **Agents do not load the rules by themselves**: the tutorial's prompt has to be pasted.
5. **A dialect cannot be shared**: there is no way to install it from a repository.
6. **Targets with emitter needs**: something that does not come out of a template (Python: single-expression
lambdas, `pass` in empty blocks) needs a new option in Rust, which only the NuclearLang team can add, never

rows.title: 004 — Backend parity: what a real API needs that the backend platform lacks — F3 — Transactions
rows.summary: DONE 2026-11-10 as ADR-0100 §4; the example below is the first idea, the delivered form is in the ADR.
body: DONE 2026-11-10 as ADR-0100 §4; the example below is the first idea, the delivered form is in the ADR.
Several repositories in one unit of work:
```nuclear
usecase MoveTask(tasks: TaskRepository, projects: ProjectRepository)
@transactional
exec(taskId: int, projectId: int) Result<AppError, Task>
project = ~projects.find(projectId)
task = ~tasks.find(taskId)
~projects.touch(project.id)
~tasks.save(task.copyWith(project = project))
`@transactional` on `exec`: the use case runs inside one transaction of the default database; an `Err` or a
thrown error rolls it back. (`fastapi`: `async with session.begin()`; `nestjs`: `sequelize.transaction` + CLS
namespace so repositories pick it up.) Done when: a test asserts a failed second write leaves the first undone.

rows.title: 005 — The language to 1.0: formatter, definitions, constructors, patterns, freeze — F3 — Named and factory constructors
rows.summary: Point x: double y: double // a named constructor: Point.origin() new origin() this(x = 0, y = 0) // a factory: computes before building new fromJson(json: <string, any>) Point Point(x = json["x"] as double, y = json["y"] as double) `new name(params)` with `this(...)` as the body is a redirecting…
body: ```nuclear
Point
x: double
y: double
// a named constructor: Point.origin()
new origin() this(x = 0, y = 0)
// a factory: computes before building
new fromJson(json: <string, any>) Point
Point(x = json["x"] as double, y = json["y"] as double)
| Dart | TypeScript | Python |
| `Point.origin() : this(x: 0, y: 0);` | `static origin(): Point { return new Point(0, 0); }` | `@classmethod def origin(cls) -> "Point": return cls(x=0, y=0)` |
| `factory Point.fromJson(...)` | `static fromJson(json): Point` | `@classmethod def from_json(cls, json)` |
`new name(params)` with `this(...)` as the body is a redirecting constructor; with a return type it is a factory.
Done when: the flutter dialect's `model` keeps generating `fromJson` and a hand-written `new` on a model is
allowed next to it (`N0xxx` when they clash).
